supported_claims.text: 武 means “military” or “martial.” It combines 戈, a weapon, with 止, originally a foot sign. Read as armed movement, the pair suggests a force setting out on campaign. The famous idea of “stopping weapons” is a later interpretation of the same visible parts.
The weapon and advancing foot contribute meaning together: armed action or a military expedition.
Pictures of a weapon and a foot combine to convey armed movement. Both are form components: the objects they depict contribute to the scene.

disagreements.text: The expedition scene is an interpretation of the weapon and foot combination. Early 止 often denotes movement, which makes that reading preferable to treating its familiar meaning “stop” as automatic proof of the original design.

limitations.text: The modern weapon part is altered; no exact stroke-movement chronology or accidental scribal corruption is established by the newly accessed article.
